title: Spring Lecture #24: Spring AOP Pointcuts & Types of Proxies

questions.question: Which pointcut matches `getStudent(Long id)` and `deleteStudent(Long id)`, but NOT `getAllStudents()` or `updateStudent(Long id, Student student)`?
options: `execution(* *(..))`: any method with any parameters
`execution(* *())`: methods with an empty parameter list
`execution(* *(*))`: methods with a single parameter of any type
`execution(* *(*, ..))`: methods with one or more parameters
questions.explanation: `(*)` means exactly one parameter of any type, so it matches the two single-argument methods only. `(..)` means zero or more parameters (matches everything), `()` means exactly zero, and `(*, ..)` means at least one, so it would also match `updateStudent(Long, Student)`.

questions.question: Given this package layout, which classes' methods are matched by `execution(* com.coderarmy.student.service.*.*(..))`?
questions.codeSnippet:
com.coderarmy.student
├── controller
│   └── StudentController
└── service
    ├── StudentService
    ├── EmailService
    └── impl
        └── PaymentServiceImpl
options: `StudentService` and `EmailService` only
`StudentService`, `EmailService` and `PaymentServiceImpl`
Only `PaymentServiceImpl`, because `*.*` means one subpackage level below `service`
Every class under `com.coderarmy.student`, including `StudentController`
questions.explanation: `service.*` matches types placed directly inside the `service` package, and the final `.*(..)` is any method with any parameters. Subpackages such as `service.impl` need `service..*`, where `..` means zero or more package segments. The controller package is never matched by a `service` prefix.

questions.question: Which of these methods are matched by `execution(* *Student(..))`?
options: All five, because each name contains "Student" or "student"
`getStudent`, `getStudentById` and `deleteStudent`
`getStudent`, `createStudentAccount`, `studentExists` and `deleteStudent`
`getStudent` and `deleteStudent` only
questions.explanation: `*Student` matches method names that END with `Student`, which is true only for `getStudent` and `deleteStudent`. `getStudentById` and `createStudentAccount` contain it in the middle (that would need `*Student*`), and name matching is case-sensitive, so `studentExists` doesn't match either.

questions.question: `@TrackExecution @Service public class StudentService extends BaseService {}`, where the unannotated `BaseService` declares `public void save()`. When `studentService.save()` is called through the proxy, which pointcut matches?
options: Both `@within(TrackExecution)` and `@target(TrackExecution)`, because the bean's class is annotated
Only `@target(TrackExecution)`, because it checks the runtime target's class, while `@within` checks the type that DECLARES `save()`
Only `@within(TrackExecution)`, because it checks the class the bean was created from
Neither, because annotations on a subclass are never visible to pointcuts
questions.explanation: `@within` looks at the declaring type of the executing method. `save()` is declared in the unannotated `BaseService`, so it does not match. `@target` looks at the class of the actual target object, which is the annotated `StudentService`, so it matches. The two often look identical and differ only in inheritance cases like this.

questions.question: An aspect uses `@Before("bean(*Service)")`. It fires for `EmailService` but never for `@Service public class StudentServiceImpl implements StudentOperations`. Why?
options: `bean()` only matches classes that do not implement an interface
`bean()` matches the simple class name, and `StudentServiceImpl` is compared without its `Impl` suffix only in XML configuration
`bean()` matches Spring bean NAMES; the default name here is `studentServiceImpl`, which does not end with `Service`
`bean(*Service)` matches only beans declared with `@Bean` methods, not component-scanned ones
questions.explanation: `bean()` is a Spring-specific designator that matches on the bean name, not the Java type. A component-scanned class gets a decapitalised default name (`studentServiceImpl`), which does not match `*Service`. Fixes include `bean(*Service*)`, naming the bean `@Service("studentService")`, or a `within()`-based pointcut.

questions.question: You want logging on every service-layer method except any method named `clearCache`. You write `within(com.coderarmy.student.service..*) && !execution(* clearCache())`. Later someone adds `clearCache(String region)`, and its calls are now being logged. What is the fix?
options: Use `!execution(* clearCache(..))`, because `()` excluded only the zero-parameter overload
Replace `&&` with `||`, since `!` binds more loosely than `&&`
Move `!execution(...)` before `within(...)`, because exclusions must come first
Use `!within(* clearCache(..))`, because `execution()` cannot be negated
questions.explanation: `()` means exactly zero parameters, so the negation removed only `clearCache()`, and the new overload still matches the `within` part. `clearCache(..)` excludes every overload. The order of `&&` operands doesn't matter, and `within()` takes type patterns, not method signatures.

questions.question: In the lecture project, `application.properties` contains `spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false`, and `StudentService` implements `StudentServiceInterface`. The controller calls `studentService.getStudent("All Student Data")`. What is printed?
options: Only `All Student Data`: the JDK dynamic proxy implements the interface but is not a `StudentService`, so `this(StudentService)` does not match
`Method Intercepted` then `All Student Data`, because the target object is a `StudentService`
`All Student Data` then `Method Intercepted`, because `this()` advice runs after the call
The application fails to start because `this()` cannot be used when `proxy-target-class=false`
questions.explanation: With `proxy-target-class=false` and an interface present, Spring creates a JDK dynamic proxy that implements `StudentServiceInterface` but does not extend `StudentService`. `this()` checks the proxy type, so it doesn't match. `target(StudentService)` would match, and with a CGLIB proxy (the Boot default) `this(StudentService)` would match too, because the proxy subclasses the class.
questions.source: code: LoggingAspect.java, application.properties, StudentService.java; notes p19-21

questions.question: With `spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false`, the lecture's controller injects `StudentServiceInterface` and works. A teammate adds a new bean whose constructor takes the concrete `StudentService` class, and the app fails at startup with a 'bean is not of required type' error. Why?
options: Spring cannot inject the same bean into two different classes
A class that implements an interface can never be injected by its class type
The `studentService` bean is an advised JDK dynamic proxy that implements only the interface, so it is not an instance of the concrete `StudentService` class
`proxy-target-class=false` disables component scanning for `@Service` classes
questions.explanation: The container exposes the proxy under the bean name. A JDK proxy is a generated class implementing the interfaces, not a subclass of `StudentService`, so injecting by the concrete type fails. Either inject the interface or use class-based (CGLIB) proxies (`proxy-target-class=true`, Spring Boot's default), which subclass the target.

questions.question: All three methods are in `in.strikes.aopDemo.service.StudentService`, and each call passes a real `Student` object. Which calls print "Student argument"?
options: Only `createStudent(s)`, because `args()` checks the declared parameter types
`createStudent(s)` and `audit(s)`
`createStudent(s)` and `updateStudent(1L, s)`
All three calls, because each passes a `Student` somewhere
questions.explanation: `args(Student)` requires exactly one argument whose RUNTIME type is compatible with `Student`. `audit(Object)` receives a `Student` at runtime, so it matches, unlike `execution(* *(Student))`, which checks the declared signature. `updateStudent` has two arguments; matching it would need `args(.., Student)` or `args(Long, Student)`.

questions.question: In the lecture's `ApplicationPointcuts` class (no `@Aspect`, no `@Component`), a developer adds `System.out.println("service layer matched")` inside the body of `@Pointcut("within(in.strikes.aopDemo.service..*)") public void serviceLayer() {}`. `LoggingAspect` uses `@Before("in.strikes.aopDemo.aspect.ApplicationPointcuts.serviceLayer()")`. What happens when a service method is called?
options: "service layer matched" is printed before every service method, then the `@Before` advice runs
Startup fails because `ApplicationPointcuts` is not annotated with `@Aspect`, so its pointcuts cannot be referenced
The `@Before` advice runs, but the println never executes, because a `@Pointcut` method is only a named declaration of the expression, never invoked as Java code
The println runs once at startup when Spring parses the expression, and never again
questions.explanation: The `@Pointcut` method just gives an expression a reusable name. Spring resolves `serviceLayer()` as a pointcut reference and never calls the method, so its body should stay empty. A plain class can hold shared named pointcuts that other aspects reference by fully qualified name; this is how the lecture's `ApplicationPointcuts` and Spring's `CommonPointcuts` example work.
